text: But Zoran Mamdani's rent freeze proved his simplified example wrong. You guys may remember this reaction from SimpleBlackTheory to my educational video on rent control, where he took our context and presented as if the video was on NYC and Mamdani's rent freeze. So in the end of my response to SBT, I said this. So how about that? Since the points that you made in your video are specifically about Mamdani and the NYC situation, let me research that topic specifically and get back to you with it. I will try to be objective, say where I think you are right and where you are wrong. It might take a couple of days, though, since from what I understand, the topic is quite nuanced. Well, since SBT did not really accept that proposal, I didn't have an obligation to research the topic. But I decided to do it anyways, partly because I was curious, partly because some of you might have expected it, partly for some other reasons. As a result, my previous two videos on this channel were specifically about NYC housing situation and Mamdani's rent freeze. Please watch them if you still didn't. Here, as mentioned in my response, I will try to quickly address SimpleBlackTheory's points. But Zoran Mamdani's rent freeze proved his simplified example wrong. My example in that video had nothing to do with Mamdani's rent freeze, so this is wrong. Moreover, Mamdani's rent freeze does not even start until October this year. So how can it prove someone right or wrong? Mamdani's rent freeze is not a blanket rent freeze on all apartments. It's for stabilized apartments, meaning that these are apartments that already have rent control on them. This is generally correct. Not to mention that the main demographic for rent-stabilized apartments in NYC are going to be lower-income minorities. So the chances of rich people grabbing rent-stabilized apartments just doesn't make any sense. This is generally wrong. Rent-stabilized tenants' demographic is pretty close to NYC renters overall. Moreover, around 30% of rent-stabilized households make over $100,000. And the system is generally not income-tested. So pretending that rich or higher-income people getting rent-stabilized apartments doesn't make sense is just wrong. He is probably confusing rent stabilization with NYCHA or public housing. He is right with the idea that we don't have enough housing for people, but we don't have enough housing because we're not having enough housing being built. Generally correct. There is more to it, though. For example, there is also empty unit problem. In 2023, NYC had about 230,000 units that were vacant but not available, including about 26,000 rent-stabilized units. Some of those are empty because of renovation costs, legal issues, seasonal use, or because the legal rent no longer makes renovation financially attractive. Research shows that rent regulations do not have any effect on new housing construction. Generally wrong. Research has found rent control can reduce rental supply, reduce mobility, reduce maintenance, and in some cases, reduce residential construction. Basic logic. If you reduce the expected return from housing construction, you usually reduce the incentive to build more of it. But the reason why we have a housing shortage is because of high interest rates, labor costs, and the cost of land as well. That is not wrong, but it is incomplete. High rates, labor, land, and construction costs matter, obviously. But pretending the shortage is only about costs ignores zoning, slow permitting, neighborhood veto power, and rules that legally block housing from being built in high-demand areas. Land is expensive partly because the city restricts how much housing can be built on it. If you make buildable land artificially scarce, congratulations, you made land more expensive. In other words, Mamdani's rent freeze is not going to negatively affect the whole housing market. The fact that not enough housing in general is being built is the problem. He is partly correct, especially about the part of the main problem is not enough housing being built. But therefore, the rent freeze has no negative effect, doesn't follow. A policy can fail to be the main cause and still make the system worse at the margins. If you are curious, this was my conclusion in yesterday's video. So overall, my conclusion is slightly different from both sides. I do not think Mamdani's rent freeze is as catastrophic as some critics say. New York's housing market is already so broken that one rent freeze is probably not going to single-handedly destroy it. But I also do not think it is as useful as supporters pretend. It helps some tenants, sure, especially people already inside the rent-stabilized system. But it doesn't solve the shortage. It leaves outsiders facing even more competition in the already brutal market. And it puts pressure on landlords, especially weaker and smaller ones. Because taxes, insurance, repairs, fuel, labor, and maintenance do not freeze just because rent does. The real solution is boring but politically painful. Build much more housing. Deregulate construction where the rules only create delays. Remove zoning limits that artificially restrict supply. Allow more density. Legalize more apartments. Speed up permits from years to months. And stop pretending that you can fix a shortage by controlling prices.
